New documentary 'Mohabat' exposes the devastating human toll of U.S. drone strikes on Afghan children who lost their fathers.
Evidence: Film clips, interviews, historical casualties
#Afghanistan #Documentary #HumanRights 🌐

Filmmaker James Longley documents 12-year-old Mohabat and other Afghan children whose fathers were killed in U.S. drone strikes and night raids.

Decades of unchecked aerial bombardment and night raids in Afghanistan left countless civilian casualties and enduring generational trauma.

Oscar-nominated filmmaker James Longley presents his new documentary 'Mohabat' at DOC NYC, chronicling the lives of Afghan youth growing up in the shadow of war.

The Bright Side:
Artistic courage brings suppressed human truths to light, forcing global audiences to confront the uncounted victims of twenty years of conflict.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing official military rhetoric with ground-level civilian survival. The film shifts focus from geopolitical abstraction to undeniable human reality.

Social Physics Analysis:
Imperial actors deployed overwhelming force under hidden pretexts, leaving civilian families to bear the wreckage. The documentary cuts through projection to reveal raw human impact.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When art confronts historical destruction with unflinching empirical truth, it bridges the gap from trauma toward moral reckoning.

The Unavoidable Truth: Civilian casualties in foreign military interventions leave generational scars that no political rhetoric can erase.

The Unavoidable Lie: Surgical military strikes eliminate targets without harming innocent families.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
“Mohabat”: New Film Follows 12-Year-Old Afghan Boy After U.S. Drone Strike Kills His Father

Oscar-nominated filmmaker James Longley talks about his new documentary Mohabat. The film is named after a 12-year-old Afghan boy whose father was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2019.

Actual Article Body:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Oscar-nominated filmmaker James Longley talks about his new documentary Mohabat, named after a 12-year-old Afghan boy whose father was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2019. Longley has filmed for years in Afghanistan both during the U.S. war and since the Taliban regained power. His previous films include Iraq in Fragments and Sari’s Mother, both of which received Academy Award nominations. His first feature-length documentary was Gaza Strip, released in 2002.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat.

ANJALI KAMAT: We turn now to the Oscar-nominated filmmaker James Longley, who’s filmed for years in Afghanistan, both during the U.S. war and since the Taliban regained power. James Longley’s new film is Mohabat. It is named after a 12-year-old Afghan boy whose father was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2019. This is a clip from the film featuring Mohabat.

MOHABAT: [translated] When the Americans came here, wherever they went, a drone was always with them. When the drone was flying, everyone was afraid. The sound of them was awful. Every person thought they would be the one targeted. I thought they would bomb me.

AMY GOODMAN: In this next clip from Mohabat, several young Afghan boys talk about how their fathers were killed during the U.S. occupation.

AFGHAN BOY 1: [translated] A night raid came. They killed my father and dragged him behind their Humvee.

AFGHAN BOY 2: [translated] My father was Taliban. I was young when he was killed.

AFGHAN BOY 3: [translated] The helicopter shot my father, and he fell out of a tree.

AFGHAN BOY 4: [translated] My father was killed by a drone strike on the second day of Eid.

AFGHAN BOY 5: [translated] My father and his friend went to fight in the war. The Americans ambushed and killed them.

AFGHAN BOY 6: [translated] It was night when they brought him home.

AFGHAN BOY 7: [translated] My father was talking on his mobile, crossing the Wardak mountains.

AFGHAN BOY 8: [translated] A drone fired at him.

AFGHAN BOY 9: [translated] They buried him with an excavator on a mountainside in Nerkh district.

AMY GOODMAN: That’s a clip from James Longley’s new documentary Mohabat. The film is having its North American premiere at the DOC NYC Film Festival here in New York this weekend. James Longley’s previous films include Iraq in...
